paragraphs.text: Between about 1000 BC and 1200 AD, the ancestors of the Polynesian peoples settled almost every habitable island in a vast triangle of the Pacific Ocean, from Hawaii in the north to New Zealand in the south-west and Easter Island in the east. They did so without metal tools, written charts or magnetic compasses, sailing double-hulled canoes across thousands of kilometres of open sea. For a long time, many European scholars refused to believe that these voyages had been deliberate.

In the 1950s, the New Zealand historian Andrew Sharp argued that the islands had been settled by accident, by canoes blown off course by storms. His view was challenged in 1976, when a reconstructed voyaging canoe called Hōkūleʻa sailed from Hawaii to Tahiti, a distance of over 4,000 kilometres, using only traditional navigation methods. The navigator on that voyage, Mau Piailug, came from Micronesia, one of the few places where such knowledge had survived.

Traditional navigators relied above all on the stars. They memorised the points on the horizon where dozens of stars rose and set, which formed a kind of 'star compass'. By steering towards a rising star until it climbed too high, and then switching to the next star that rose at the same point, a navigator could maintain a steady course throughout the night.

During the day, and when clouds hid the stars, other signs were used. Navigators could identify the direction of the main ocean swells, which can remain constant for days, by the movement of the canoe beneath them; some were said to lie down in the hull to feel them more precisely. As they approached land, they watched for birds such as terns and noddies, which fly out to sea to feed in the morning and return to land in the evening. Clouds that formed over islands and changes in the colour of the sea also indicated land beyond the horizon.

This knowledge was passed down orally, often within families, through years of training. Much of it disappeared after contact with Europeans, as colonial governments and missionaries discouraged traditional practices and modern ships replaced canoes. Since the voyage of Hōkūleʻa, however, there has been a remarkable revival, and a new generation of Pacific navigators has completed voyages around the world without instruments.
